title: Chapter 5 — Of Property
paragraphs: We may consider natural reason, which tells us that men, once born, have a right to their preservation, and so to food and drink and whatever else nature provides for their subsistence. Or we may consider revelation, which gives us an account of the grants God made of the world to Adam, and to Noah and his sons. Either way it is very clear that God, as King David says (Psal. cxv. 16), “has given the earth to the children of men” — given it to mankind in common. But once this is assumed, some people find it very hard to see how anyone could ever come to have a property in anything. I will not be content with answering that, if it is hard to explain property on the assumption that God gave the world to Adam and his descendants in common, it is impossible for any man except one universal monarch to have any property on the assumption that God gave the world to Adam and his heirs in succession, to the exclusion of all the rest of his descendants. Instead I shall try to show how men might come to have a property in separate parts of what God gave to mankind in common, and that without any express agreement of all the commoners.

God, who has given the world to men in common, has also given them reason to make use of it to the best advantage of life and convenience. The earth and everything in it is given to men for the support and comfort of their existence. All the fruits it naturally produces, and the beasts it feeds, belong to mankind in common, since they are produced by the spontaneous hand of nature; and no one originally has a private dominion over any of them, excluding the rest of mankind, while they remain in this natural state. Yet since they are given for men to use, there must necessarily be some means of appropriating them in one way or another before they can be of any use, or any benefit at all, to a particular man. The fruit or venison that feeds the wild Indian, who knows no enclosure and is still a tenant in common, must be his — and so much his, that is, so much a part of him, that no one else can any longer have any right to it — before it can do him any good in sustaining his life.

Though the earth and all lower creatures are common to all men, every man has a property in his own person. Nobody has any right to this but himself. The labour of his body and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his. So whatever he removes from the state that nature has provided and left it in, he has mixed his labour with, and joined to it something that is his own, and in this way he makes it his property. Since he has removed it from the common state nature placed it in, his labour has attached something to it that excludes the common right of other men. For this labour is unquestionably the labourer’s property, so no one but he can have a right to what it has once been joined to — at least where there is enough, and as good, left in common for others.

A man who lives on the acorns he picked up under an oak, or the apples he gathered from the trees in the wood, has certainly appropriated them to himself. Nobody can deny that the nourishment is his. So I ask: when did they begin to be his? When he digested them? When he ate them? When he boiled them? When he brought them home? Or when he picked them up? It is plain that if the first gathering did not make them his, nothing else could. That labour marked them off from what was common. It added something to them beyond what nature, the common mother of all, had done, and so they became his private right. Will anyone say he had no right to the acorns or apples he appropriated in this way because he did not have the consent of all mankind to make them his? Was it robbery to take for himself what belonged to everyone in common? If consent like that were necessary, man would have starved, despite all the plenty God had given him. We see in commons that remain common by agreement that it is the taking of any part of what is common, and removing it from the state nature leaves it in, that begins property; without that, the common is of no use. And taking this part or that does not depend on the express consent of all the commoners. So the grass my horse has eaten, the turf my servant has cut, and the ore I have dug in any place where I have a right to them in common with others become my property, without anyone else assigning them to me or consenting to it. The labour that was mine, in removing them from the common state they were in, has fixed my property in them.

If the explicit consent of every commoner were required before anyone could appropriate any part of what is given in common, children or servants could not cut up the meat their father or master had provided for them in common without first assigning each person his own portion. The water running in the fountain is everyone’s, yet who can doubt that the water in the pitcher belongs only to the man who drew it out? His labour has taken it out of the hands of nature, where it was common and belonged equally to all her children, and in doing so has appropriated it to him.

So this law of reason makes the deer belong to the Indian who has killed it. It is accepted as the goods of the man who has spent his labour on it, even though before it was everyone’s common right. And among those counted the civilized part of mankind, who have made and multiplied positive laws to determine property, this original law of nature for the beginning of property in what was previously common still applies. By virtue of it, any fish a man catches in the ocean — that great common of mankind which still remains — or any ambergris he picks up here, becomes the property of the one who took the trouble over it, through the labour that removes it from the common state nature left it in. Even among us, the hare that someone is hunting is considered to belong to the man who pursues her during the chase. For since she is an animal still regarded as common, and no man’s private possession, whoever has spent enough labour on any animal of that kind to find and pursue her has thereby removed her from the state of nature, in which she was common, and has begun a property.

It may perhaps be objected that if gathering acorns or other fruits of the earth gives a right to them, then anyone may hoard up as much as he likes. I answer: not so. The same law of nature that gives us property in this way also sets limits to that property. “God has given us all things richly” (1 Tim. vi. 12) is the voice of reason confirmed by inspiration. But how far has he given them to us? To enjoy. As much as anyone can make use of to any advantage of life before it spoils, so much he may fix a property in by his labour. Whatever goes beyond this is more than his share and belongs to others. Nothing was made by God for man to spoil or destroy. So, considering how plentiful natural provisions were for a long time in the world, how few people there were to consume them, and how small a part of that provision one man’s industry could reach and hoard up to the harm of others — especially if he kept within the limits reason sets on what might serve his use — there could then be little room for quarrels or disputes about property established in this way.

But the chief matter of property now is not the fruits of the earth and the beasts that live on it, but the earth itself, since that takes in and carries with it all the rest. I think it is plain that property in land, too, is acquired in the same way as the former. As much land as a man tills, plants, improves and cultivates, and can use the produce of, is his property. By his labour he, as it were, encloses it from the common. Nor will it undermine his right to say that everyone else has an equal title to it, so that he cannot appropriate or enclose it without the consent of all his fellow commoners, that is, all mankind. When God gave the world in common to all mankind, he also commanded man to labour, and the poverty of man’s condition required it of him. God and his reason commanded him to subdue the earth — that is, to improve it for the benefit of life — and in doing so to invest in it something that was his own: his labour. Whoever, in obedience to this command of God, subdued, tilled and sowed any part of it thereby attached to it something that was his property, to which no one else had any title, and which no one could take from him without injury.

Nor did this appropriation of any plot of land by improving it harm any other man, since there was still enough, and as good, left — more than those not yet provided for could use. In effect, then, there was never any less left for others because he had enclosed some for himself. For a man who leaves as much as another can make use of does as well as if he took nothing at all. Nobody could think himself injured by another man’s drinking, even if he took a long drink, when he himself had a whole river of the same water left to quench his thirst. And the case of land and water, where there is enough of both, is exactly the same.

God gave the world to men in common. But since he gave it to them for their benefit, and for the greatest conveniences of life they could draw from it, we cannot suppose he meant it always to stay common and uncultivated. He gave it for the use of the industrious and rational (and labour was to be their title to it), not to the whims or greed of the quarrelsome and contentious. A man who had as good land left for him to improve as what was already taken had no need to complain, and ought not to interfere with what had already been improved by another’s labour. If he did, it is plain that what he wanted was the benefit of another’s efforts, to which he had no right, and not the ground God had given him in common with others to work on — ground of which there was as good left as what was already occupied, and more than he knew what to do with, or than his industry could reach.

It is true that in land that is common in England, or in any other country where there are plenty of people living under government who have money and commerce, no one can enclose or appropriate any part without the consent of all his fellow commoners. That is because it is left common by compact, that is, by the law of the land, which must not be violated. And though such land is common with respect to some men, it is not common to all mankind; it is the joint property of this country, or this parish. Besides, what remained after such an enclosure would not be as good for the rest of the commoners as the whole was when they could all use the whole. But in the beginning, when the great common of the world was first being peopled, it was quite otherwise. The law man lived under then was rather in favour of appropriating. God commanded him to labour, and his needs forced him to. Wherever he had fixed his labour, that was his property, which could not be taken from him. And so we see that subduing or cultivating the earth and having dominion over it are joined together; the one gave title to the other. So God, by commanding man to subdue the earth, gave him authority to appropriate to that extent. And the condition of human life, which requires labour and materials to work on, necessarily brings in private possessions.

Nature has set the measure of property well, by the extent of men’s labour and the conveniences of life. No man’s labour could subdue or appropriate everything, and no man’s enjoyment could consume more than a small part. So it was impossible for any man in this way to encroach on another’s right, or to acquire a property to the harm of his neighbour, who would still have room for as good and as large a possession (after the other had taken his) as there was before the appropriation. In the first ages of the world, this measure kept every man’s possession to a very modest size — such as he could appropriate without injuring anybody — for then men were more in danger of getting lost by wandering away from their company in what was then the vast wilderness of the earth than of being short of room to plant. And the same measure may still be allowed without harm to anyone, full as the world seems. For suppose a man, or a family, in the condition men were in when the world was first peopled by the children of Adam or Noah, and let him plant in some vacant inland part of America. We shall find that the possessions he could make for himself, by the measures we have given, would not be very large, and even today would not harm the rest of mankind, or give them reason to complain or think themselves injured by this man’s encroachment — even though the human race has now spread to every corner of the world and vastly exceeds the small number there was at the beginning. Indeed, land in itself is worth so little without labour that I have heard it claimed that even in Spain a man may be allowed to plough, sow and reap without being disturbed on land he has no other title to than the fact that he is using it. On the contrary, the inhabitants think themselves indebted to a man who, by his industry on neglected and therefore waste land, has increased the stock of corn they lacked. But however that may be — I lay no weight on it — this I dare boldly affirm: the same rule of property, namely that every man should have as much as he could make use of, would still hold in the world without leaving anyone short, since there is land enough in the world for twice the number of its inhabitants, if the invention of money, and men’s tacit agreement to put a value on it, had not introduced (by consent) larger possessions and a right to them. How it has done this I shall shortly show at greater length.

This much is certain. In the beginning, before the desire to have more than man needed had altered the intrinsic value of things, which depends only on their usefulness to human life, or before men had agreed that a little piece of yellow metal, which would keep without wasting or decaying, should be worth a large piece of meat or a whole heap of corn, men did have a right to appropriate by their labour, each for himself, as much of the things of nature as he could use. Yet this could not be much, nor could it harm others, where the same plenty was still left to those who would put in the same industry. Let me add that a man who appropriates land to himself by his labour does not reduce the common stock of mankind but increases it. For the provisions that support human life produced by one acre of enclosed and cultivated land are (to put it very conservatively) ten times more than those yielded by an acre of equally rich land lying waste in common. So a man who encloses land, and gets a greater plenty of the conveniences of life from ten acres than he could have from a hundred left to nature, may truly be said to give ninety acres to mankind. For his labour now supplies him from ten acres with provisions that used to be the produce of a hundred lying in common. I have rated the improved land very low here, making its yield only ten to one, when it is much nearer a hundred to one. For I ask whether, in the wild woods and uncultivated waste of America, left to nature without any improvement, tillage or husbandry, a thousand acres yield their needy and wretched inhabitants as many conveniences of life as ten acres of equally fertile land do in Devonshire, where they are well cultivated?

Before land was appropriated, whoever gathered as much wild fruit, or killed, caught or tamed as many beasts, as he could — whoever spent his efforts on any of the spontaneous products of nature in such a way as to alter them from the state nature had put them in, by applying some of his labour to them — thereby acquired a property in them. But if they perished in his possession without being properly used — if the fruit rotted or the venison went bad before he could consume it — he offended against the common law of nature and was liable to be punished. He had invaded his neighbour’s share, because he had no right to any of them beyond what his use required and what might serve to provide him with the conveniences of life.

The same measures governed the possession of land as well. Whatever he tilled and harvested, stored and used before it spoiled, was his own particular right. Whatever land he enclosed, and could graze and make use of, the cattle and the produce were also his. But if the grass in his enclosure rotted on the ground, or the fruit of his planting perished without being gathered and stored, this part of the earth, despite his enclosure, was still to be regarded as waste, and might become the possession of anyone else. So at the beginning Cain might take as much ground as he could till and make it his own land, and still leave enough for Abel’s sheep to graze on; a few acres would serve for both their possessions. But as families grew, and industry increased their stocks, their possessions grew with their need of them. Even so, this was usually without any fixed property in the ground they used, until they formed communities, settled together and built cities. Then, by consent, they came in time to mark out the bounds of their separate territories, agree on boundaries between themselves and their neighbours, and settle by their own laws the properties of the members of the same society. For we see that in the part of the world first inhabited, and therefore likely to be the most populous, even as late as Abraham’s time people wandered freely up and down with their flocks and herds, which were their wealth; and Abraham did this in a country where he was a stranger. From this it is plain that at least a large part of the land lay in common, and that the inhabitants did not value it or claim property in any more than they used. But when there was not enough room in the same place for their herds to graze together, they separated by consent, as Abraham and Lot did (Gen. xiii. 5), and extended their pasture wherever it suited them best. And for the same reason Esau left his father and his brother and settled in Mount Seir (Gen. xxxvi. 6).

And so, without supposing that Adam had any private dominion and property over the whole world, excluding all other men — which cannot be proved in any way, nor can anyone’s property be derived from it — but supposing that the world was given, as it was, to the children of men in common, we see how labour could give men distinct titles to separate plots of it for their private uses. In this there could be no doubt about right, and no room for quarrels.

Nor is it as strange as it may perhaps seem before we think about it that the property of labour should be able to outweigh the community of land. For it is labour, indeed, that makes the difference in value in everything. Let anyone consider the difference between an acre of land planted with tobacco or sugar, or sown with wheat or barley, and an acre of the same land lying in common without any cultivation on it, and he will find that the improvement made by labour accounts for by far the greater part of the value. I think it would be a very modest estimate to say that, of the products of the earth useful to human life, nine tenths are the effects of labour. Indeed, if we value things correctly as they come to our use, and add up the various costs spent on them — what in them is purely owing to nature and what to labour — we shall find that in most of them ninety-nine hundredths must be wholly put down to labour.

There could be no clearer proof of this than various nations of the Americans. They are rich in land and poor in all the comforts of life. Nature has supplied them as generously as any other people with the materials of plenty — that is, a fruitful soil, able to produce in abundance whatever might serve for food, clothing and pleasure. Yet because they do not improve it by labour, they do not have a hundredth part of the conveniences we enjoy; and the king of a large and fruitful territory there is fed, housed and clothed worse than a day labourer in England.

To make this a little clearer, let us just trace some of the ordinary provisions of life through their various stages before they come to our use, and see how much of their value they receive from human industry. Bread, wine and cloth are things in daily use and great plenty. Yet if labour did not supply us with these more useful commodities, acorns, water and leaves or skins would have to be our bread, drink and clothing. For whatever bread is worth more than acorns, wine more than water, and cloth or silk more than leaves, skins or moss, is owed entirely to labour and industry. The one set is the food and clothing that unaided nature provides for us; the other is the provisions that our industry and effort prepare for us. When anyone has calculated how much the latter exceed the former in value, he will see how much labour makes up by far the greatest part of the value of the things we enjoy in this world. The ground that produces the materials is hardly to be counted in at all, or at most only as a very small part — so small that even among us, land left wholly to nature, with no improvement by pasture, tillage or planting, is called waste, as indeed it is; and we shall find its benefit amounts to little more than nothing.

This shows how much a large population is to be preferred to large territories, and that the increase of lands and the right use of them is the great art of government. And a prince who is so wise and godlike as to secure, by established laws of liberty, protection and encouragement for the honest industry of mankind against the oppression of power and the narrowness of party will soon be too strong for his neighbours. But this is by the way.
To return to the argument at hand.

An acre of land here that bears twenty bushels of wheat, and another in America that would do the same with the same husbandry, undoubtedly have the same natural, intrinsic value. Yet the benefit mankind receives from the one in a year is worth £5, and from the other possibly not worth a penny, if all the profit an Indian got from it were valued and sold here; at least, I can truly say, not a thousandth part as much. It is labour, then, that puts the greatest part of the value on land, without which it would hardly be worth anything. It is to labour that we owe the greatest part of all its useful products. For everything by which the straw, bran and bread from that acre of wheat are worth more than the produce of an acre of equally good land lying waste is entirely the effect of labour. It is not merely the ploughman’s effort, the reaper’s and thresher’s toil and the baker’s sweat that must be counted into the bread we eat. The labour of those who broke in the oxen, who dug and worked the iron and stones, who felled and shaped the timber used for the plough, the mill, the oven or any of the other tools — and they are a vast number — needed for this corn, from its being seed to be sown to its being made into bread, must all be charged to the account of labour and recognized as its effect. Nature and the earth supplied only the materials, which in themselves are almost worthless. If we could trace them, it would be a strange list of the things that industry provided and used for every loaf of bread before it came to our use: iron, wood, leather, bark, timber, stone, bricks, coal, lime, cloth, dyes, pitch, tar, masts, ropes, and all the materials used in the ship that brought any of the commodities used by any of the workmen in any part of the work. It would be almost impossible, or at least too long, to list them all.

From all this it is evident that, although the things of nature are given in common, man, by being master of himself and owner of his own person and of its actions or labour, still had within himself the great foundation of property. And what made up the greater part of what he used for the support or comfort of his existence, once invention and the arts had improved the conveniences of life, was entirely his own and did not belong in common to others.

So in the beginning labour gave a right of property wherever anyone chose to apply it to what was common; and what was common remained for a long time by far the greater part, and is still more than mankind makes use of. At first men were for the most part content with what unaided nature offered for their needs. Later, in some parts of the world, where the growth of population and stock, together with the use of money, had made land scarce and so of some value, the various communities settled the bounds of their separate territories, and by their own laws regulated the properties of the private men of their society; and so, by compact and agreement, they settled the property that labour and industry had begun. And the leagues made between various states and kingdoms, expressly or tacitly disowning all claim and right to the land in the other’s possession, have by common consent given up their claims to the natural common right they originally had to those countries, and so have settled by positive agreement a property among themselves in distinct parts and parcels of the earth. Yet even so, there are still great tracts of land to be found which lie waste (their inhabitants not having joined the rest of mankind in consenting to the use of their common money). These lands are more than the people who live on them do or can make use of, and so they still lie in common — though this can hardly happen among the part of mankind that has consented to the use of money.

Most of the things really useful to human life — the things the need to survive made the first commoners of the world look for, as it does the Americans now — are generally things that do not last long; if they are not used up, they decay and perish of themselves. Gold, silver and diamonds are things whose value comes from fancy or agreement rather than from real use and the necessary support of life. Now, of the good things nature has provided in common, everyone had a right (as has been said) to as much as he could use, and a property in everything he could bring about with his labour: everything his industry could reach, to alter it from the state nature had put it in, was his. A man who gathered a hundred bushels of acorns or apples thereby had a property in them; they were his goods as soon as they were gathered. He had only to make sure that he used them before they spoiled; otherwise he took more than his share and robbed others. And indeed it was foolish, as well as dishonest, to hoard more than he could use. If he gave part of them away to someone else, so that they did not perish uselessly in his possession, this too was making use of them. And if he traded plums that would have rotted in a week for nuts that would stay good to eat for a whole year, he did no injury. He did not waste the common stock, or destroy any part of the share of goods that belonged to others, as long as nothing perished uselessly in his hands. Again, if he chose to give his nuts for a piece of metal because he liked its colour, or to exchange his sheep for shells, or his wool for a sparkling pebble or a diamond, and to keep these by him all his life, he did not invade the right of others. He might pile up as much of these durable things as he pleased, since going beyond the bounds of his just property lay not in the size of his possessions but in letting anything perish uselessly in them.

And this is how money came into use: some durable thing that men could keep without its spoiling, and that by mutual consent they would accept in exchange for the truly useful but perishable necessities of life.

And just as different degrees of industry tended to give men possessions in different proportions, so this invention of money gave them the opportunity to keep and enlarge them. For suppose there were an island, cut off from all possible trade with the rest of the world, with only a hundred families on it. Suppose it had sheep, horses and cows, and other useful animals, wholesome fruits, and enough land for corn for a hundred thousand times as many people, but nothing on the island fit to serve as money, because everything there was either too common or too perishable. What reason could anyone there have to enlarge his possessions beyond what his family could use, and a plentiful supply for its consumption — whether from what their own industry produced, or from what they could get by bartering with others for similarly perishable, useful goods? Where there is not something that is both lasting and scarce, and so valuable enough to be hoarded, men will not tend to enlarge their holdings of land, however rich it may be and however free they are to take it. For I ask: what value would a man put on ten thousand, or a hundred thousand, acres of excellent land, already cultivated and well stocked with cattle, in the middle of the inland parts of America, where he had no hope of trade with other parts of the world to bring him money by selling the produce? It would not be worth enclosing, and we would see him give back to the wild common of nature whatever was more than would supply him and his family with the conveniences of life available there.

So in the beginning all the world was America, and more so than America is now, for no such thing as money was known anywhere. Find something that has the use and value of money among his neighbours, and you will see the same man at once begin to enlarge his possessions.

But gold and silver are of little use to human life compared with food, clothing and transport, and get their value only from men’s consent, though labour still largely sets the measure of it. So it is plain that men have agreed to an unequal and disproportionate possession of the earth. By a tacit and voluntary consent they have found a way in which a man may fairly possess more land than he himself can use the produce of: he receives gold and silver in exchange for the surplus, and these can be hoarded without injury to anyone, since these metals do not spoil or decay in the hands of the person who has them. Men have made this division of things into unequal private possessions workable outside the bounds of society, and without compact, simply by putting a value on gold and silver and tacitly agreeing to use money. For under governments, the laws regulate the right of property, and the possession of land is determined by positive constitutions.

And so, I think, it is very easy to see, without any difficulty, how labour could at first begin a title of property in the common things of nature, and how spending it on our uses set limits to that title. So there could then be no reason to quarrel over title, nor any doubt about how large a possession it gave. Right and convenience went together. For as a man had a right to everything he could apply his labour to, so he had no temptation to labour for more than he could make use of. This left no room for disputes about title, nor for encroaching on the rights of others. The portion a man cut out for himself was easy to see, and it was pointless, as well as dishonest, to cut out too much for himself, or take more than he needed.
